sql_theory_p1: > SQL injection is the modification of a database query via user input when data is concatenated into an SQL string without isolation.
sql_theory_p2: > Classic example: code concatenation like query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE login = """ + login + """" — live SQL enters the login field.
sql_theory_p3: > Login bypass: a quote closes the string, then OR 1=1 makes the condition always true; comment characters (--, #) truncate the original query.
sql_theory_p4: > UNION SELECT combines results of two SELECT queries; number and types of columns must match — otherwise an error occurs (often determined by ORDER BY n).
sql_theory_p5: > In MySQL, information_schema (tables, columns) system views help discover DB structure without direct file access.
sql_theory_p6: > Blind / time-based SQLi: application response doesn't show rows, but delays (SLEEP) or a "yes/no" response difference still leak data.
sql_theory_p7: > Main application-level defense: parameterized queries (prepared statements): placeholders, separate value transfer, no interpolation into SQL text.
sql_theory_p8: > OWASP classifies injections as A03: 2021 Injection; combine validation, least privilege principle in DB, and monitoring for anomalous queries.

xss_theory_p1: > XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) — injecting executable code (usually JavaScript) into a page viewed by another user.
xss_theory_p2: > Reflected — payload "reflects" in server response; Stored — saved on server and shown to many; DOM-based — client-side JS error parsing URL/data.
xss_theory_p3: > Without proper escaping, tags and attributes (script, img onerror, svg onload, javascript: in href) can lead to code execution in page context.
xss_theory_p4: > HttpOnly on cookies complicates session hijacking via document.cookie, but doesn't negate other XSS effects (DOM manipulation, actions on behalf of user).
xss_theory_p5: > Content-Security-Policy restricts script sources and reduces inline JS execution probability; combine with validation and contextual encoding.
xss_theory_p6: > Context matters: escaping for HTML, attributes, JS strings, and URLs differs; the same string can be safe in one place and dangerous in another.

csrf_desc: Cross-site request forgery attacks on authenticated sessions.
csrf_theory_p1: > CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) — an attacker tricks a user into performing an unwanted action on another site where they are authenticated.
csrf_theory_p2: > Mechanism: User is authenticated on bank.com. Attacker sends a link to malicious-site.com. Malicious site makes a request to bank.com via the user's browser.
csrf_theory_p3: > The browser automatically sends cookies (session token) with the request. The bank sees an authenticated user and performs the action (money transfer, password change).
csrf_theory_p4: > The vulnerability arises because the bank cannot verify that the request originated from a legitimate user action.
csrf_theory_p5: > Defense: CSRF tokens (random, per-form/session), SameSite cookie attribute, Origin/Referer header checks, POST requests only.
csrf_theory_p6: > SameSite attribute prevents cookies from being sent on cross-site requests; set to Strict or Lax.
csrf_lvl1_ex: Example: Browser loads image and silently sends an authenticated request.
csrf_lvl2_ex: Hidden form automatically submitted to perform complex actions (POST data with multiple parameters).
csrf_lvl3_ex: GET parameter triggered on image load, video fallback, or automatic iframe refresh.
path_desc: Directory traversal attacks to access files outside the target directory.
path_theory_p1: > Path Traversal — an attacker uses ../ sequences to navigate to parent directories and access protected files.
path_theory_p2: > Example: Application allows /downloads?file=readme.txt but is vulnerable to: /downloads?file=../../../etc/passwd
path_theory_p3: > Exploits lack of validation or incomplete filters. A simple blacklist for ../ can be bypassed via URL encoding.
path_theory_p5: > Accessible files: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /var/log/*, config files, .env, DB backups, source code.
path_theory_p6: > Defense: Whitelist allowed files, chroot/jail access, absolute paths, validation without ../, disable directory listing.
path_lvl1_ex: Basic: Simply use ../ to ascend directories to root, then navigate to target (/etc/passwd).
path_lvl2_ex: When ../ is blocked, use encoding: %2e%2e%2f or ..%2f or variations like %252e instead of %2e.
path_lvl3_ex: Combine multiple bypass techniques: partial hex encoding %2e%2e, UTF-8 variations, multiple slashes, etc.
auth_desc: Password guessing attacks, token manipulation, and session hijacking.
auth_theory_p1: > Authentication Bypass — bypassing login using weak passwords, token manipulation, or predictable session generation.
auth_theory_p2: > Category 1: Brute Force — attacker tries common passwords (password123, admin, letmein) until one works.
auth_theory_p3: > Category 2: JWT Manipulation — if the server doesn't verify the signature, an attacker can modify the token (change admin:false to admin:true) and re-encode it.
auth_theory_p4: > Category 3: Session Prediction — if tokens are weakly generated (timestamp, user_id, random 4-digit), an attacker can guess the next one.
auth_theory_p5: > Defense: Strong password requirements, rate limiting on login attempts, proper JWT signature verification with a secret, secure random generation.
auth_theory_p6: > Additionally: Multi-factor authentication (2FA), lockout after N attempts, HTTPS for transport, secure session management.
auth_lvl1_ex: Brute force common weak passwords: admin/admin, admin/password, admin/123456
auth_lvl2_ex: JWT format: header.payload.signature. Modify payload: {"admin": true}. Base64 encode. Server accepts if signature not verified.
auth_lvl3_ex: Token patterns: username_timestamp, MD5(user_id), incremental IDs. Guess based on known user data.

auth.1: JWT-structure: header.payload.signature. Header contains algorithms and token type.
auth.2: JWT-signature: created using HMAC with secret key. Without the secret, signature cannot be forged.
auth.3: Password-reset: tokens must be unpredictable and expire quickly. Using timestamps or UUID.
auth.4: Session-management: cookies should have HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes.
auth.5: 2FA: adds second layer of protection. Even with password, attacker needs second factor.
auth.6: Rate-limiting: prevents brute force attacks by limiting attempts per time period.

xss.1: Reflected XSS: malicious script executes when user visits vulnerable URL. Script reflects in response.
xss.2: Stored XSS: malicious script saved in database and executes for all users viewing the content.
xss.3: DOM-based XSS: vulnerability in client-side JavaScript. Script manipulates DOM to execute malicious code.
xss.4: XSS prevention: output encoding converts special characters to HTML entities. Prevents script execution.
xss.5: CSP headers: restrict script sources. Whitelist approach prevents loading unauthorized scripts.
xss.6: XSS payload: <script>alert('XSS')</script> basic test. More advanced: img onerror, svg onload, etc.

sql.1: SQL injection: malicious SQL code inserted into query. Can bypass authentication, extract data.
sql.2: UNION-based: combines results from multiple tables. Requires same column count and compatible types.
sql.3: Blind SQL: no visible output. Use time delays (SLEEP) or conditional responses to extract data.
sql.4: SQL prevention: parameterized queries separate SQL code from data. Input validation and escaping.
sql.5: ORM protection: object-relational mapping automatically escapes inputs. Still need validation.
sql.6: Error-based: trigger database errors that leak information. Use functions like extractvalue(), updatexml().

csrf.1: CSRF attack: forces victim to perform unwanted actions on authenticated website. Uses social engineering.
csrf.2: CSRF tokens: random values tied to user session. Prevents state-changing requests without proper token.
csrf.3: SameSite cookies: restrict cookie sending based on site context. Strict/Lax/None modes control behavior.
csrf.4: Referer checking: validates HTTP Referer header to ensure request came from same origin. Can be bypassed.
csrf.5: Double Submit Cookie: token stored in cookie and request parameter. Server compares both values.
csrf.6: CSRF prevention: combine multiple defenses - tokens, SameSite, Origin checks, custom headers.

path.1: Directory traversal: ../ sequences move up one level. Can access files outside the root directory.
path.2: URL encoding: %2F = /, %2E = ., %5C = \. Bypasses filters that check literal characters.
path.3: Double encoding: %252F = %2F = /. Bypasses filters with single decoding.
path.4: Input validation: whitelist of allowed files, check file extensions, use chroot jail.
path.5: File access permissions: limit web server user access. Use principle of least privilege.
path.6: Path normalization: resolve all path components before validation. Prevents bypass techniques.

sql_level1_simple_theory: Imagine a website asks for login and password. SQL injection is when you write clever code instead of a password that tricks the database. The database thinks: 'Ah, the password matches!' and lets you in. Try entering: ' OR '1'='1 — this is like saying 'or truth equals truth', which is always true!
sql_level2_simple_theory: A database is like a giant table with columns and rows. Imagine a student table: name, surname, grade. UNION allows you to join two tables into one. If a website shows products from the 'products' table, we can add data from the 'users' table using UNION — and see passwords! The important thing is that the number of columns must match.
sql_level3_simple_theory: Sometimes a website doesn't show data directly, but you can ask it questions that it answers with 'yes' or 'no'. For example: 'Is there an admin in the database with a password starting with letter A?' If the page loads slowly — that means yes! This way you can guess the entire password letter by letter. It's like playing 'guess the word'.
xss_level1_simple_theory: XSS is like graffiti on a website, but instead of paint you use code. Reflected XSS — when the code is in the URL or form, and the server shows it immediately. Imagine a site that writes 'Hello, [name]!' If instead of a name you enter <script>alert('Hacked!')</script>, the browser will execute this code!
xss_level2_simple_theory: Stored XSS — when your graffiti code is saved on the server forever. Imagine a chat or comments section. You write malicious script in a comment, it gets saved in the database, and now everyone who opens that page will run your code! This is more dangerous than Reflected because it attacks all users.
xss_level3_simple_theory: DOM-based XSS — when the website changes right in your browser without the server. Imagine a site that takes text from the URL (#something) and puts it on the page. If the site doesn't check this text, you can insert a script! The server doesn't see anything bad, but code executes in the browser. This is the sneakiest type of XSS.
csrf_level1_simple_theory: CSRF is like a substitution trick. You log into your bank website (and you're already authorized). Then you open an email with an image, but actually the image is a button saying 'transfer money to scammer'. Your browser automatically sends a request to the bank with your cookies! The bank thinks you pressed it yourself.
csrf_level2_simple_theory: To protect against CSRF, websites add a secret token to every form. This is like a special password that only the real website knows. If a request comes without the token — the website rejects it. But what if the token is predictable? Or what if the website checks the token but you can bypass the check?
csrf_level3_simple_theory: SameSite cookie is a new protection in browsers. The cookie is marked as 'Strict' or 'Lax', and the browser won't send it to other websites. But what if the site uses old cookies without SameSite? Or what if you can bypass this protection through timing or other vulnerabilities?
path_level1_simple_theory: Path Traversal is like running through floors of a building. A website should only show files from its own folder (for example, /www/images/). But if you write ../../../etc/passwd instead of a filename, we climb 3 floors up and land in the system folder! This allows reading any files on the server.
path_level2_simple_theory: Websites try to protect themselves by blocking words like '../'. But you can trick them! For example, use '..%2f' — where %2f is an encoded slash /. Or use double encoding: %252f becomes %2f, then /. The filter passes it through, but the server still moves to another folder!
path_level3_simple_theory: Some websites check file extensions — for example, only allowing .jpg and .png. But you can use null byte (%00) or other tricks! For example, file.jpg%00.txt — the server sees .txt and allows it, but actually opens file.jpg, and when processing the null byte it cuts off everything after it.
auth_level1_simple_theory: Brute Force is a 'brute strength' method. Imagine you have a safe with a 4-digit code. You try 0000, 0001, 0002... until it opens. It's the same with passwords! There's a list of most popular passwords: password, 123456, qwerty. Many people use simple passwords, and they're easy to guess with a program.
auth_level2_simple_theory: A JWT token is like a pass with a signature. The website gives you a token containing information (who you are, what rights you have) and a signature confirming authenticity. But what if the signature is weak? Or what if the website checks the signature incorrectly? You can modify the token (for example, make yourself an admin) and sign it with your own signature!
auth_level3_simple_theory: A reset token is a code for resetting your password that comes to your email. It should be random and long so it can't be guessed. But sometimes developers make it predictable: user number + current date. Or it never expires — you can use an old token months later!

sql_context_1: The recently activated authentication system contains a vulnerability. Your task is to log in as administrator without knowing the password. The system runs on MySQL. This could change everything.
sql_context_2: The system has started blocking your requests. A WAF (Web Application Firewall) was detected. You'll need clever tricks: alternative symbols, encoding, obfuscation. Normal techniques won't work anymore.
sql_context_3: You've penetrated the system, but the database is protected. You need to know its structure: how many columns, which tables, what data. Start by enumerating columns. Every successful query brings you closer to the goal.
sql_context_4: The structure is known. Now it's time to see system information: MySQL version, environment variables, other metadata. UNION SELECT will allow you to combine your query with system data.
sql_context_5: The main node is compromised, but that's not all. The system has hidden tables with sensitive data. You need to find information_schema and get the complete list of database tables.
sql_context_6: Final stage. You know table names, structure, access rights. Now you just need to extract the FLAG — the ultimate confirmation that you completely control the system. It will be costly, but it's worth it.
